---
title: "Quiz: shape features"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A disc and a five-pointed star have the same area. Name two features that tell them apart, and two that do not.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which features depend only on how much and how spread out, and which on the outline?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Apart: solidity (the star has large concave gaps: about 0.5 against 1), form factor (long perimeter), max/min Feret, inscribed radius. Not apart: area and equivalent diameter (equal by construction), and the eigenvalues: both have $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, so eccentricity 0.
:::

---

**Q2.** Two touching round nuclei were segmented as one object. Which shape feature flags it, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the outline look like where they touch?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Solidity: the outline has two concave notches at the neck, so the convex hull is noticeably larger than the object (0.92 against 0.96 for a single digital disc in the demo). The area (twice a nucleus) and the eccentricity help too.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why is the form factor $4\pi A/P^2$ of a large digital disc about 0.62 when the perimeter is the pixel-edge count?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The edge count is too long by a constant factor.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The edge count is $4/\pi$ times the true perimeter, so $P^2$ is $(4/\pi)^2$ times too large and the form factor $(\pi/4)^2 = \pi^2/16 \approx 0.62$ instead of 1, at every resolution.
:::

---

**Q4.** A small round object of about 30 pixels gets a form factor of 1.3. Is it "more circular than a circle"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which perimeter estimate was used?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: for every shape the true value is at most 1. The perimeter estimate is too short (the chain code through pixel centres runs half a pixel inside the true boundary, a large fraction for a small object), so $4\pi A/P^2$ comes out too large. For objects of a few pixels the form factor is not meaningful.
:::

---

**Q5.** What is the difference between the max Feret diameter and the major axis length $4\sqrt{\lambda_1}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One depends on two extreme points, the other on all pixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The max Feret is the largest distance between two points of the object (a geometric extreme: one protruding pixel changes it). The major axis is the length of the equivalent ellipse, computed from the variance of all pixels (robust to a single pixel, but it is a summary that need not touch the outline: for a rectangle it is longer than the rectangle).
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does the rotating-calipers method only need the hull vertices, and why is the minimum width always found with one caliper flush with a hull edge?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do supporting lines touch a set?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A supporting line of the object is also a supporting line of its convex hull, and it touches the hull at a vertex (or along an edge), so only hull vertices matter. Between two directions where the touching vertices change, the width is $c\,|\cos(\theta - \varphi)|$, a concave function; its minimum on the interval is at an end, i.e. where a caliper lies along an edge.
:::

---

**Q7.** A rod of width 10 µm and length 50 µm. Estimate its maximum inscribed radius and its min Feret. What happens to both if the rod is bent into a C?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of the two "sees" the bend?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Straight: inscribed radius ≈ 5 µm, min Feret ≈ 10 µm. Bent into a C: the inscribed radius stays ≈ 5 µm (it is a thickness), while the min Feret grows a lot (the calipers must span the curve).
:::

---

**Q8.** The pixels of a microscope stack are 0.2 µm wide but the slices are 1 µm apart. What goes wrong if you measure 3D shape features in voxel units?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a sphere look like in voxel units?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Distances along $z$ are counted 5 times too short: a sphere looks like a flattened ellipsoid, so volume, surface, Feret diameters, eccentricity and compactness are all wrong, and orientation is biased. Compute in physical coordinates $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)$, or resample to isotropic voxels first.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Use the shoelace formula to compute the area of the triangle $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(1, 3)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\frac12\sum (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\frac12\big[(0\cdot 0 - 4 \cdot 0) + (4 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 0) + (1 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 3)\big] = \frac12 \cdot 12 = 6$, as $\frac12 \cdot$ base $4 \cdot$ height 3.
:::
